summary: North light at the end of the Burlington, Vermont breakwater on Lake Champlain: wooden lights from the 1850s, an 1890 north light, a 1925 skeletal tower and a 2004 replica.

lens.where: beacon lights of the 1886-1890 period (NRHP); sixth-order lenses on the 1857 wooden towers (LighthouseFriends)

light.note: Focal plane 35 ft (about 11 m) above the water per LighthouseFriends and Wikipedia; the station record's 12.2 m is not confirmed. The US Lighthouse Society's 2004 Light List entry reads Fl W 2.5s; the station record reads Fl R 2.5s; neither was checked against a current Light List.

structures.type: wooden tower at the north end
structures.note: LighthouseFriends: wooden towers placed on both ends in 1857; the northern tower burned in 1870. The nomination instead dates lighthouses at each end to 1886.

structures.type: wooden tower on the detached section
structures.note: Lights placed at both ends of the detached section when it was completed in 1890 (LighthouseFriends); replaced in 1925.

structures.type: skeletal steel tower with tank house
structures.note: LighthouseFriends dates the skeletal towers to 1925; the nomination dates the modern metal light towers to about 1960.

structures.type: replica of the c.1890 tower, steel frame clad in wood
structures.note: Built by Atlantic Mechanical of Wiscasset, Maine, to a design based on photographs; activated with the south light on 12 September 2004 (LighthouseFriends). The station record and Wikipedia give 2003.

staffing.note: Lights were lit by hand for the last time in 1938 (LighthouseFriends); automatic lights did not appear until 1938 (nomination).

access.note: Tower closed. A public fishing pier, reached by Lake Street, gives a good view of the light (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Wooden towers placed at the ends of the breakwater (LighthouseFriends). The nomination gives 1886 for lighthouses at each end.
Lighthouses built at each end; signal lanterns replaced by beacons with a Fresnel lens (nomination). Conflicts with the 1857 date.
North beacon discontinued on 22 October 1890 (Lighthouse Board, fiscal 1891); lights placed at both ends of the detached section that year (LighthouseFriends).
Beacon on the old north end moved to the north end of the north extension (Lighthouse Board, fiscal 1891).
A new beacon built at the north extension (Lighthouse Board, fiscal 1893).
Wooden towers replaced by skeletal towers with tank houses (LighthouseFriends). The nomination dates the modern metal towers to about 1960.
Lights manually lit for the last time in 1938 (LighthouseFriends); automatic lights from 1938 (nomination).
Replica towers activated on 12 September 2004 (LighthouseFriends). The station record and Wikipedia give 2003.
High water removed the lower skirting from the north tower; not replaced as of 2014 (LighthouseFriends).

wrecks.outcome: Schooner driven onto the southern end of the breakwater with five people aboard; all reached the wall and were taken off by a Burlington man in a rowboat. The schooner was never raised.

corrections.proposed: to be checked against the current Light List
corrections.why: The Society's entry for the 2004 Light List reads Fl W 2.5s. Wikipedia gives red for the current light; the record's source is not read here.
LighthouseFriends gives the north light's focal plane as 35 feet above the water (about 10.7 m); Wikipedia also gives 35 feet.
LighthouseFriends gives the activation date as 12 September 2004 and says the north light began to flash the same night. Wikipedia gives 2003 and is not used as a source.

corrections.proposed: 1857 for the first wooden towers; the current tower is a 2004 replica of the c.1890 tower
corrections.why: The record's built date applies to the first wooden tower, which burned in 1870. The standing tower is a replica.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends dates the replicas' activation to 12 September 2004; the station record gives 2003 from the Light List. Wikipedia gives 2003 in the text and 2004 in its infobox for the south light. The story gives the 2004 ceremony and marks the record's year as different.

The record gives 1857 for the standing tower. The nomination gives lighthouses at each end in 1886; LighthouseFriends gives 1857 for the first wooden towers and says the northern one burned in 1870. The story gives both.
LighthouseFriends dates the keeper's dwelling to 1875; the nomination dates the prefabricated house to 1874. The story gives both.
LighthouseFriends dates the skeletal towers to 1925; the nomination dates the modern metal towers to about 1960. Both are reported; neither is corroborated by a third source here.

The US Lighthouse Society roster says James Wakefield, Jr. (1873-1890); LighthouseFriends says Sr. The 1876 newspaper names Mr. James Wakefield with one of his sons. The nomination calls the 1876 rescuer a ship chandler, while LighthouseFriends calls him the keeper. The story does not identify the rescuer with the keeper.

notes_for_editor: 1) Build dates conflict: LighthouseFriends (1857 wooden towers at both ends, after $2,000 appropriated in 1854; northern tower burned 1870; detached section lights 1890; skeletal towers 1925; replicas activated 12 Sept 2004) vs the nomination (first lantern 1842 kept by a steamboat company; lighthouses at each end 1886; modern towers about 1960). The Light-House Board volumes support an 1890 north beacon discontinued 22 Oct 1890 and a beacon moved to the north end of the north extension. The 1891 volume also records a fog bell at 'Burlington Breakwater, north end, October 21, 1890' in its fog-signal list, but the OCR is too poor to quote; LighthouseFriends dates a south-end bell to 21 Oct 1907. Check the page images before printing either. 2) James Wakefield: roster says 'Jr.' (1873-1890), LighthouseFriends says 'Sr.', the 1876 newspaper names him with one son, and the nomination calls him a ship chandler. The story does not link the 1876 rescuer to the keeper. 3) Roster lists a contractor, James E. Cashman, with no years; he is not a keeper and is left out of the keepers list. 4) Roster begins 1856; the first lights are dated 1857 by LighthouseFriends. Not resolved. 5) Characteristic and range: the station record gives Fl R 2.5s, 12 nm and focal height 12.2 m; the Society's 2004 Light List entry prints Fl W 2.5s; LighthouseFriends gives a 35-foot focal plane. Not checked against a current Light List, so no characteristic or range is printed in the story. 6) Keeper for 1938 last manual lighting: LighthouseFriends gives Hill's span as 1937-1938, the roster 1937-1939. 7) The Burlington Weekly Free Press OCR is poor ('tho', 'Irom'); quotes are copied from the OCR as it stands. The rescuer's name in OCR is 'Wakelield'. 8) Searches: two Chronicling America searches for the 1876 wreck and one for 1930s breakwater lighting (no hits). The 1938 automation and the 1925 towers rest on LighthouseFriends and the nomination only; no newspaper confirmed them. 9) Wikipedia (lead only) says 'activated on September 12, 2003' in one place and 'lit in 2004' in its infobox. Not cited. 10) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story's keeper sentence now gives Tibbetts 1867-1870 and Bliss 1870-1873 as the roster prints them; the 1893 beacon is cited as the fiscal-1893 report; the 1896-97 beacon item is cited to the volume labelled 1896-1897 (scan page 68, read through the corpus, page confirmed by the archive index with no question mark); the 1891 North Beacon discontinuance (22 October 1890) is in the report's LIGHTS DISCONTINUED list on scan page 18.
